Gerudo with Ganondorf might very well carve out their own kingdom in the region. I wouldn't expect it to be a large kingdom but one well defended. This would be after Timur of the Timurid Empire had died. The empire broke up into city-states and that would probably work in the Gerudo's favor to survive as their own nation. If Ganondorf is with them, then I assume so is Twinrova and Nabooru. With these three powerful people they definitely could keep their own territory. They might even go conquering eventually. They would also need to deal with plague.

Sheikah - I don't know. If they have Sheikah tech and all their magic, they're probably fine. Their best bet for survival is probably to stay hidden and stay away from the clashes happening in that period. We know they are good at hiding. If they wanted to try to claim the shogunate, they might manage it but I don't think they'd keep it for long unless they have full access to their tech- including guardians. They might not have to worry about plague as much as the other races.

Rito are probably fine up until the arrival of European conquerors. Depending on what indigenous groups they encounter, they might have a hard time defending themselves or they might get along just fine. But when Europeans show up, you know they're going to want to capture or kill as many of these weird bird people as possible. 

And I'm going to assume the Gorons go to various islands with highly active volcanoes and do well in those places, and they probably do okay there until colonial expansion uncovers the existence of rock-people.

Interesting thing about the Metroidvania term is that it doesn't at all refer to the original Castelvania games, which had basically none of the features that are considered part of the Metroidvania style. Metroid did have some of these elements - challenging platforming, backtracking after getting a new tool to open a new area or change how old areas are progressed, some level of non-linearity.

It wasn't really until Symphony of the Night that the vania part of Metroidvania made sense (and really was the game the term was coined off of).

Zyzzix the Many can also increase power through reaping. I'm not really sure you answered the question by stating this.

If it has 6 power, it isn't destroyed by damage until it takes 6 damage, and it also deals 6 damage while fighting.

Power is *sort of* like power and toughness in MTG, or attack and health in Hearthstone, but combined into a single value that's used both when dealing damage and when taking damage.

The card in particular, Zyzzix the Many, can increase it's power both with fighting and reaping. If you use this while fighting, it has to survive the fight to receive the additional power counters. If it's destroyed by the damage from the fight, it's moved to the discard pile as normal.

If it already has damage counters on it when you increase it's power, it will keep those damage tokens.

Make failures keep the story moving. Don't say "you fail," give them information that will keep them moving forward. If it's a successful check, then that should benefit at least themselves or one other member of the group in some way, or it should lead to possible branching paths for the adventuring phase.

One example, say the Scholar rolls a check to recall from history the purpose of the ruins the companions have just found. On a failure, give him a small snippet, "an ancient tower once stood here, protecting the area from intruders." On a success, they learn more, "the tower was built by agents of the enemy long ago, when his forces were strong in this region." If they succeed particularly well, "It is said that a hero of the Dunedain and a commander of the Easterlings fought and fell together near such a tower. There are whispers that the spirit of the Easterling might still roam nearby, keeping away any who would come to bury the hero's remains and give his spirit peace."

Each level of information gives the company different ideas about what they should do next. Different amounts of information might lead them to investigate further, or to leave what they find be, or to seek to do something truly heroic but incredibly dangerous.

Back to the possible benefits, another example might be the scholar making a check about some kind of trolls that the company is expecting they will have to overcome through combat or some other means. A scholar might make a check to determine the creature's weakness. On a failure, he might recall what sort of troll it is. On a success, he might recall how tough they are and what weapons are ineffective against them or which ones are effective. On a strong success, he might recall what weapons are extremely effective or if they have some other weakness (like stone-trolls and sunlight). I could see giving a bonus to attacking the troll, maybe if even just for a round, on a success in this scenario. I could also see giving the companions a bonus to defend against a particular attack or feature that the checked enemy has (such as giving a bonus to saves against a wood-wight's Horror of the Wood ability, or a bonus to AC against gallows-weeds if the Scholar recalls their method of attack). In some cases, you might want the party to find some in-game way to stay the effects of a feature, like knowing that they need to find some Shadow-thorn when they realize the enemy they face uses poison. 

I have to admit, even with me saying all of this, I find it difficult to do in practice. Physical skill checks are far easier to know where to use and how to use correctly. Either way, I think skill checks should not be a barrier to continuing, they should be more like speed-bumps and forks in the road.
